parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Explain the main principles behind the use of ultrasound to obtain diagnostic information about internal body structures.

markscheme_points.text: * produced by quartz crystal / piezo-electric crystal
* gel / coupling medium (on skin) used to reduce reflection
reflected pulse / wave detected by (ultrasound) transmitter
* intensity of reflected pulse / wave gives information about
* time delay gives information about depth of boundary
max. 2 of additional detail points marked *

hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about what kind of sound signal is sent into the body - is it continuous or sent in short bursts, and why would bursts be useful for timing?
Hint 2: Think about how that high-frequency sound is made and also detected - what special crystal property lets electrical signals turn into vibrations and back again?
Hint 3: Remember what happens when sound tries to go from air or the probe into skin - why is a gel put on the skin first?
Hint 4: Picture the inside of the body as layers of different tissues - what happens to a sound wave when it meets a boundary between two different media?
Hint 5: Think about the two pieces of information carried by each returning echo - what could its arrival time tell you, and what could its size tell you?
Hint 6: Finish by considering what must happen to all those returning electrical signals so a doctor can actually see an image of the structures.
parts.proper_answer: A short pulse of ultrasound is produced by a piezo-electric (quartz) crystal transducer. Coupling gel is used on the skin to reduce reflection at the skin surface. The pulse is partially reflected at boundaries between different tissues. The reflected pulse is detected by the same transducer. The time delay gives the depth of the boundary and the intensity gives information about the tissues. Signals are processed and displayed to form an image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Making a Short Pulse**
Think of ultrasound imaging like sonar or an echo sounder. You do not send a continuous sound, you send a very short pulse of ultrasound, typically in the MHz range. A short pulse is essential because you need a clear start time so you can time how long the echo takes to come back.

Step 2: **The Piezo-electric Transducer Does Two Jobs**
That pulse is made by applying a rapidly alternating voltage to a piezo-electric crystal, often quartz. The crystal vibrates at ultrasonic frequency and emits the sound wave. The clever part is that the same crystal works in reverse as a detector. When a returning echo squeezes it, it generates a small voltage. So one probe is both transmitter and receiver.

Step 3: **Getting the Sound Into the Body**
Ultrasound reflects very strongly at an air-skin boundary because of the large acoustic mismatch. That would mean almost no energy enters the body. To fix this, a coupling medium or gel is spread on the skin. It excludes air and matches impedances better, so transmission into tissue is greatly improved.

Step 4: **Reflections Inside the Body**
As the pulse travels through soft tissue, whenever it meets a boundary between different media, for example muscle to bone or tissue to fluid, part of the energy is reflected and part continues. It is these partial reflections or echoes that carry the diagnostic information.

Step 5: **What Time and Size Tell You**
Two things are measured for each echo. The time delay between transmission and detection tells you how deep the boundary is, using $$s = \frac{v t}{2}$$ where $v$ is the speed of ultrasound in tissue and division by 2 is for the go-and-return journey. The intensity of the reflected pulse tells you about the nature of the boundary and the tissues, because a larger acoustic mismatch gives a stronger reflection.

Step 6: **Building the Image**
The detected echoes are converted back to electrical signals, amplified, processed and displayed, for example as an A-scan trace or a B-scan image. A complete scan builds up a picture of the positions and types of internal structures.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A parallel beam of ultrasound has intensity $I_0$ as it enters a muscle of thickness $4.6\text{ cm}$, as illustrated in Fig. 4.1.

{{figure:figure_4_1}}

The intensity of the beam just before it leaves the muscle is $I_{\text{T}}$. The ratio $I_0/I_{\text{T}}$ is found to be 2.9.

Calculate the linear attenuation (absorption) coefficient $\mu$ of the ultrasound in the layer of muscle.
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 4.1 - intensity falls from $I_0$ to $I_T$ over a known thickness $x = 4.6\text{ cm}$. Think about the general shape of absorption loss - linear or exponential with distance?

Hint 2: Recall the exponential attenuation law linking transmitted intensity $I_T$, incident intensity $I_0$, thickness $x$ and coefficient $\mu$, then rearrange to make $\mu$ the subject using natural logs.
Hint 3: Use the given ratio $I_0/I_T = 2.9$ to avoid needing $I_0$ and $I_T$ separately, and check your final unit is $\text{cm}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **The Attenuation Law**
As a parallel beam passes through tissue, its intensity is absorbed and scattered exponentially, not linearly. The governing relation is $$I_T = I_0 \exp(-\mu x)$$ where $I_0$ is incident intensity, $I_T$ is transmitted intensity, $x$ is thickness and $\mu$ is the linear attenuation coefficient.

Step 2: **Rearrange Using the Ratio**
Divide by $I_0$ and invert to use the given ratio: $$\frac{I_T}{I_0} = \exp(-\mu x)$$ $$\frac{I_0}{I_T} = \exp(\mu x)$$ Take natural log of both sides: $$\ln\left(\frac{I_0}{I_T}\right) = \mu x$$ Here $x = 4.6\text{ cm}$ and $I_0/I_T = 2.9$, so $$2.9 = \exp(4.6\mu)$$

Step 3: **Calculate mu**
Solving for $\mu$: $$\mu = \frac{\ln(2.9)}{4.6}$$ $$\mu = \frac{1.0647}{4.6} \approx 0.23\text{ cm}^{-1}$$ A positive value with unit $\text{cm}^{-1}$ is expected because $x$ was in cm.
